case_name: Prasad @ Hari Prasad Acharya v State of Karnataka
respondent:
State of Karnataka
Supreme Court of India

9 February 2009
Criminal Appeal No. 242 of 2009(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 5271 of 2008)
The Judgment was delivered by : Dr. Arijit Pasayat, J.
1. Leave granted.
2. Challenge in this appeal is to the judgment of a learned Single Judge of the Karnataka High Court upholding the conviction of the appellant for offence punishable under Sections 447, 376(2)(g) and 506 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (in short the 'IPC'). Various custodial sentences were imposed on the appellant and one Sathish.
3. It is not necessary to refer to the factual aspects in detail in view of the order proposed to be passed.

facts: On 30.4.2003 around midnight both the accused persons went to the house of the victim, the prosecutrix (PW-1). They called out her husband. He came out after lighting the kerosene lamp and found the accused persons. The prosecutrix was compelled by the accused persons to follow them to the jungle and she was threatened that if she did not do so her hut would be set on fire. When she refused, they forcibly took her about 100 ft. away from the hut and forcibly committed rape on her and threatened not to disclose to anybody.
After the incident PWs 1 and 2 went and informed one Santosh Hegde (PW-7) who told them to give a police complaint.
On 1.5.2003 at about 9.00 p.m. First Information Report was lodged.
The prosecutrix was subjected to medical examination and the same indicated that she was subjected to sexual intercourse around 12 hours prior to the time of examination.
issues: Challenge in this appeal is to the judgment of a learned Single Judge of the Karnataka High Court upholding the conviction of the appellant for offence punishable under Sections 447, 376(2)(g) and 506 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (in short the 'IPC').
petitioner_arguments: The evidence has not been discussed and abrupt conclusions have been arrived at about the guilt of the accused.
respondent_arguments: Supported the judgments of the trial Court and the High Court.
court_reasoning: The absence of reasons has rendered the High Court's judgment not sustainable.

Reasons introduce clarity in an order. On plainest consideration of justice, the High Court ought to have set forth its reasons, howsoever brief, in its order indicative of an application of its mind.
Failure to give reasons amounts to denial of justice.
holding: The appeal is allowed to the aforesaid extent.
